approachQuestion.prompt:
Shared inspection access

Two teams provide closed access windows A and B. Within each list the windows are sorted by start and strictly separated: one end is less than the next start. Return the sorted maximal closed windows during which both teams have access. A single shared endpoint is a valid one-point window. Do not modify either list.

Input: A = [[1,4],[8,12]], B = [[3,9],[12,15]]
Output: [[3,4],[8,9],[12,12]]

Input: A = [[2,3]], B = [[5,8]]
Output: []

Constraints: 0 ≤ m,n ≤ 200000, where m and n are the lengths of A and B; integer endpoints satisfy 0 ≤ start ≤ end ≤ 1000000000. Both lists support indexed reads. The output contains new records. Among methods with best worst-case running time, prefer the least auxiliary memory, excluding output.

options.text: Keep one index per list. For the current pair, emit [max(starts), min(ends)] if the lower bound is at most the upper bound. Advance the window with the smaller end; advance both if the ends are equal.
options.feedback: Once a window ends, later windows in the other list cannot create a new intersection with it. Advancing the earlier end safely discards only an exhausted candidate.

options.text: Copy both lists into temporary arrays, then use two indices, emitting each valid intersection and advancing whichever current window ends first, or both on a tie.
options.feedback: The intersection rule and advancement are correct for all inputs, but the supplied lists already support the required reads. Copying both lists adds removable memory and copying work.

options.text: Emit the intersection of the current pair if nonempty, then advance the window with the larger end; advance both on a tie.
options.feedback: For A=[[1,10]] and B=[[2,3],[5,6]], advancing A after the first match misses [5,6]. The longer-lived window may still intersect later windows.

options.text: Use two indices and advance the earlier end, but emit an intersection only if max(starts) is strictly less than min(ends).
options.feedback: For A=[[1,4]] and B=[[4,7]], the required result is [[4,4]]. Strict comparison incorrectly drops this closed one-point intersection.

feedback.reason: Discard an interval only after its end makes all further intersections impossible.
details: Keep two forward indices. Compare the current windows, emit their nonempty closed intersection, and discard the earlier-ending window, discarding both on a tie. Write directly into a preallocated returned array with capacity m+n and a logical length. No temporary copies or recursive calls are used.

Closed intervals intersect even at a single shared endpoint. After emitting max(starts)..min(ends), discard the earlier-ending window because it cannot reach a later partner. Equal ends permit discarding both.

Copying both lists adds removable memory and copying work.

“Emit the intersection of the current pair if nonempty, then advance the window with the larger end; advance both on a tie.”: For A=[[1,10]] and B=[[2,3],[5,6]], advancing A after the first match misses [5,6]. The longer-lived window may still intersect later windows.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For advance-earlier-end, analyze the worst case as a function of the two list lengths m and n. The returned array has capacity m+n and a logical length, with no final copying step. Choose the tightest standard time and auxiliary-space pair for nonempty lists.
constraints: Analyze only the named method. Count all temporary arrays and the call stack; exclude the supplied input and returned output. Numeric comparisons, assignments and arithmetic take constant time, with no overflow.
No hashing or amortized data structure is used. All loops and binary searches are iterative; there is no recursive stack.

options.text: Time O((m+n) log(m+n)), auxiliary space O(m+n)

feedback.reason: At least one input index advances at each comparison.
details: Each comparison advances at least one index, so there are at most m+n advances. Interleaved windows can require a linear number of comparisons and emitted intersections. The two indices and endpoint variables use constant auxiliary memory. The returned array is excluded; neither input is copied.
Worst case over nonempty lists; iterative two-index scan; returned capacity m+n excluded.
“Time O(mn), auxiliary space O(1)”: The two indices move monotonically; pairs are not enumerated independently, so a product bound is not tight.
“Time O(m+n), auxiliary space O(m+n)”: The returned array is excluded. The method retains only two indices and endpoint variables, rather than copying both lists.
“Time O((m+n) log(m+n)), auxiliary space O(m+n)”: The inputs are already sorted and never re-sorted. Each index advances only forward.
